power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: The dynamical systems approach is gaining attention across many subfields of clinical psychology.
Although the systems are assumed to involve many variables, theoretical and methodological work in this field often relies on low-dimensional stability landscapes, creating potential mismatches.

In this article, I discuss how high-dimensional stability landscapes may challenge intuitions derived from low-dimensional landscapes, put forward a potential solution based on sufficient low-dimensional descriptions, and propose a future research agenda centered on dimensionality reduction approaches that emphasize preserving information about stability and transitions.

Dynamical systems research has a long tradition in psychopathology, and it is gaining attention in recent years, especially in clinical and behavioral changes (e.g., Olthof et al., 2023; Öngür & Paulus, 2024; Schüler et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Dynamical systems research has a long tradition in psychopathology, and it is gaining attention in recent years, especially in clinical and behavioral changes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Olthof et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Öngür & Paulus, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Schüler et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Common themes stressed in these fields are dynamic attractors formed from complex interactions and reinforcement of all elements at different levels.
These attractors are relatively stable.
Once a person is in one attractor, whether that is depression, aggressive behavior, or self-achievement, the person tends to stay there as if there is a force pulling the person back.
Although transitions between attractors are not easy, they may still happen and correspond to important psychological processes, such as onset, recovery, and relapse.
Therefore, the dynamical systems perspective emphasizes the role of stability and transitions in psychopathology.

Despite the common interests in diverse disciplines, I found that much recent theoretical work from dynamical systems assumes a low-dimensional structure in the stability landscape: when using an illustration with stability landscapes, it is drawn in a space with two or three dimensions.
Methodological work that calculates stability landscapes from data (e.g., Cui et al., 2026) also produces output in a low-dimensional space.
text.formatted: Methodological work that calculates stability landscapes from data (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Cui et al., 2026)</ref> also produces output in a low-dimensional space.

text.text: This may not align with the systematic approach assumed at the beginning, which involves multiple elements, thus high-dimensional.
Is this a problem or not?
One may argue that the landscape plots are simply lower-dimensional illustrations.
The actual stability landscape lives in high-dimensional space, but we draw the landscape in lower-dimensional space for visualization.
However, problems arise when we look into high-dimensional stability landscapes, which is considerably different from intuitions based on low-dimensional landscapes (Wales, 2018).
text.formatted: However, problems arise when we look into high-dimensional stability landscapes, which is considerably different from intuitions based on low-dimensional landscapes <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Wales, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: First, in high-dimensional space, the local minima are often not separated by high barriers (Draxler et al., 2018; Gordon, 1991).
text.formatted: First, in high-dimensional space, the local minima are often not separated by high barriers <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Draxler et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Gordon, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Many paths exist between a pair of local minima, requiring less effort for transitions.
This conflicts with the common use of stability landscapes in conceptualizing psychopathology, where stable minima represent psychological phases, and barriers are hard to climb over.
Second, distances between observations in high-dimensional spaces can become very similar, making it hard to distinguish nearby from distant states (Beyer et al., 1999).
text.formatted: Second, distances between observations in high-dimensional spaces can become very similar, making it hard to distinguish nearby from distant states <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Beyer et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: This also conflicts with intuition in low dimensions, that states in the depressive basin are similar to each other and different from states in the healthy basin.
Taken together, if the stability landscape does live in a high-dimensional space, its inferred properties do not align well with clinical phenomena motivated from low-dimensional intuitions.

To resolve these conflicts, I propose that, although mental states live in a high-dimensional space (i.e., with many variables), we can still sufficiently describe the stability and transitions with fewer dimensions (Tenenbaum et al., 2000; also see Kheirkhah et al., 2026, for a similar view originating from neuroscience and AI).
text.formatted: To resolve these conflicts, I propose that, although mental states live in a high-dimensional space (i.e., with many variables), we can still sufficiently describe the stability and transitions with fewer dimensions <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Tenenbaum et al., 2000</ref>; also see <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Kheirkhah et al., 2026</ref>, for a similar view originating from neuroscience and AI).

text.text: This is because the number of variables we can use to describe a state is different from the number of coordinates we need to involve.

Consider the geographic location of any points on the surface of Earth: the Earth lives in three-dimensional space, so we can describe any geographical location with its three-dimensional coordinates, but actually we only need to involve two coordinates (longitude and latitude) to pinpoint a location.
In psychopathology, several reasons may contribute to this distinction.
First, many psychological measures intrinsically overlap or correlate with one another.
For example, in a questionnaire, one may be asked to rate their level of sadness, desperation, and concentration.
The answers, although appearing as different variables in data, are not fully independent.
For example, the meaning of sadness and desperation overlaps, and when one is sad, it makes it harder to concentrate as well.
Second, biological constraints of humans also limit the possible trajectory of mental states, reducing the range of possible states.
For example, a person cannot constantly stay in a state with extreme physiological arousal, which places substantial demands on the body's resources.
Third, although some variables in intensive longitudinal assessments are important in characterizing a person's current state, they are not key variables for a person's course of mental disorder.
An example is who accompanies the person.

Although social supports are important in mental disorders, if a person is in contact with a close friend in the morning but stays alone in the afternoon, it does not mean the person's severity of mental disorder has changed substantially.
Assuming the stability landscape can be described with fewer coordinates does not mean these coordinates are easy to find and easily interpretable.
Therefore, I propose a three-step direction for future research.
In the first step, researchers should identify the key coordinates through dimensionality reduction.

In contrast to traditional dimensionality reduction approaches that prioritize maximizing explained variance, the suitable approach in this proposal should best preserve the stability and transition structures relevant to psychopathology.
After that, dynamical systems modeling can be applied in these new coordinates, yielding the dynamical rules.
Finally, the phenomena in this low-dimensional space should also be connected back to the original variables, making the results interpretable.

In this way, researchers would not need to describe the full stability landscape in high-dimensional space, which is difficult both practically and methodologically, and the curse of dimensionality can be transformed into an actionable agenda.
